items.title: Microbiology of pyogenic liver abscess
items.contentHtml:
Microbiología

  • Escherichia coli es el germen más común en absceso hepático piógeno, seguido de Klebsiella pneumoniae (endémico en Asia, asociado a hiperviscosidad).
  • La vía biliar ascendente favorece polimicrobianos: enterobacterias, enterococos y anaerobios.
  • En hemocultivos, Escherichia coli se aísla en ~30-50% de casos, pero el cultivo de aspirado es más sensible.
  • En pacientes con inmunosupresión o neutropenia, considerar Candida spp. o Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Trampa de examen: Klebsiella pneumoniae puede causar absceso hepático sin foco biliar, a menudo en diabéticos, con tendencia a metástasis sépticas.

items.title: Vías de diseminación y fisiopatología
items.contentHtml:
Routes of dissemination

  • The most common route is the biliary portal (ascending from cholangitis or cholecystitis), followed by the portal route (pylephlebitis due to diverticulitis or appendicitis).
  • The arterial route (bacteremia) and contiguity (visceral perforation) are less common.
  • The Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, abdominal pain) suggests cholangitis as the origin, not an isolated abscess.
  • The single abscess is usually right (greater right portal flow), but the bile duct produces multiple abscesses.
  • Portal seeding occurs due to septic thrombophlebitis of the portal vein, with secondary hepatic infarcts that become infected.

items.foco: Presentación: fiebre y dolor en hipocondrio derecho
items.title: Síntomas y signos clave
items.contentHtml:
Clinical presentation

  • The classic triad includes fever, pain in the right upper quadrant and hepatomegaly, but it only appears in ~50% of cases.
  • Fever is the most constant symptom (>90%); It may be the only finding in the elderly or immunosuppressed.
  • The pain is dull, continuous, with radiation to the right shoulder due to diaphragmatic irritation.
  • There may be nausea, weight loss or jaundice (the latter suggests biliary obstruction or severe sepsis).
  • The absence of fever does not rule out the diagnosis; In diabetics the presentation can be subacute with only general discomfort.

items.title: Ultrasound as a first study
items.contentHtml:
Diagnostic imaging

  • Abdominal ultrasound is the initial test of choice due to its availability and low cost; sensitivity ~80-90% for single abscesses.
  • Key finding: hypoechoic, well-defined lesion, with irregular borders and possible internal echoes (pus); may show gas if anaerobes are present.
  • Limitation: small (<2 cm) or multiple abscesses may be missed; CT is superior in these cases.
  • Ultrasound also evaluates bile duct (dilation, stones) to identify origin.
  • If ultrasound is negative but suspicion is high, do not delay the tomography.

items.foco: CT with contrast: portal phase for abscesses
items.title: CT scan and phases
items.contentHtml:
Computed tomography

  • CT with contrast is the diagnostic gold standard; sensitivity >95%.
  • The portal phase (delay ~70 seconds) is optimal because the liver parenchyma enhances and the abscess appears as a hypodense lesion.
  • Key finding: hypodense collection with peripheral ring enhancement (ring sign) after contrast, sometimes with internal gas.
  • The arterial phase may show early peripheral enhancement, but the portal phase defines the better the collection.
  • Tomography also detects multiple abscesses, gas, and complications such as rupture or portal thrombosis.

items.foco: Image-guided percutaneous drainage: treatment of choice
items.title: Percutaneous drainage and invasive management
items.contentHtml:
Invasive treatment

  • Image-guided percutaneous drainage is the treatment of choice for single or multiple accessible abscesses, combined with antibiotics.
  • Indications: abscess >5 cm, failure to antibiotics alone within 48-72 hours, or suspected complication.
  • Percutaneous catheter drainage is preferable to simple aspiration, with high success rates. ~85-90%.
  • Surgery (laparotomy or laparoscopy) is reserved for rupture of the peritoneum, failure of percutaneous drainage, or multiple non-drainable abscesses.
  • Aspirate culture should always be obtained before starting antibiotics, if possible.

items.foco: Empirical antibiotic therapy: ceftriaxone plus metronidazole
items.title: Initial antibiotic regimen
items.contentHtml:
Antibioticoterapia empírica

  • El esquema empírico de elección es ceftriaxona más metronidazol, cubriendo enterobacterias y anaerobios.
  • Dosis típicas: ceftriaxona 2 g intravenoso cada 24 horas y metronidazol 500 mg intravenoso cada 8 horas.
  • Alternativas: piperacilina-tazobactam o carbapenem (si hay riesgo de Klebsiella productora de betalactamasas de espectro extendido o enfermedad grave).
  • Si el origen es biliar, considerar agregar cobertura para enterococo (ampicilina) en pacientes críticos.
  • La duración total de antibióticos es de 2-4 semanas, con vía intravenosa inicial seguida de oral según evolución.

items.foco: Complicación: empiema o ruptura a peritoneo
items.title: Complicaciones graves y manejo
items.contentHtml:
Complicaciones

  • La ruptura a peritoneo causa peritonitis difusa, con dolor abdominal generalizado y signos de irritación peritoneal; requiere drenaje quirúrgico urgente.
  • El empiema (derrame pleural infectado) ocurre por extensión transdiafragmática; se diagnostica por toracocentesis y requiere drenaje pleural.
  • Otras complicaciones: sepsis, bacteriemia, trombosis de vena porta (pileflebitis) y abscesos metastásicos.
  • La ruptura a peritoneo tiene mortalidad alta; la tomografía muestra contigüidad con la cápsula hepática y líquido libre.
  • En caso de empiema, el tratamiento incluye antibióticos y drenaje con tubo torácico, no solo antibióticos.

items.title: Criptogénico y diabetes
items.contentHtml:
Cryptogenic origin

  • When no biliary or portal focus is identified, it is considered cryptogenic; in these cases diabetes mellitus should be ruled out.
  • Diabetes mellitus predisposes to liver abscess due to Klebsiella pneumoniae, often without apparent bile duct.
  • In diabetics, the presentation may be more indolent and with a greater risk of septic complications.
  • Cryptogenic evaluation includes blood cultures, biliary ultrasound, and ruling out immunosuppression or malignancy. occult.
  • If the patient has de novo hyperglycemia, request glycated hemoglobin for diagnosis of diabetes mellitus.

items.foco: Absceso amebiano: diferenciar por serología y aspecto de anchoa
items.title: Differential diagnosis with amoebic abscess
items.contentHtml:
Amebic vs pyogenic differentiation

  • The amoebic abscess is associated with Entamoeba histolytica; the typical aspirate has an anchovy appearance (chocolate pus, without a foul odor).
  • Serology for amoeba (indirect hemagglutination or enzyme immunoassay) is positive in >90% of amoebic abscesses.
  • The pyogen is usually single, with a positive culture and higher fever; amoebic is more common in young men, travelers or immigrants.
  • Tomography does not differentiate reliably; Serology and culture are key.
  • Amebic treatment is metronidazole (does not require routine drainage if it is <5 cm and without complications).

items.title: Culture and antibiogram
items.contentHtml:
Aspirate culture

  • The aspirate culture (obtained during percutaneous drainage) is essential to guide definitive antibiotic therapy.
  • It should be sent in bottles for aerobes, anaerobes and, if suspected, fungi.
  • The results allow the spectrum to be adjusted, reducing resistance and toxicity; example: if sensitive Klebsiella pneumoniae grows, it can be de-escalated from ceftriaxone to first-generation cephalosporin.
  • Negative culture occurs in ~20-30% of cases, especially if antibiotics have already been administered; does not delay drainage.
  • Gram stain of the aspirate provides immediate guidance: gram-negative bacilli suggest enterobacteria.

items.foco: Higher mortality in: multiple abscesses or sepsis
items.title: Prognosis and risk factors
items.contentHtml:
Prognosis

  • Mortality is higher in multiple abscesses or sepsis at diagnosis, reaching up to 10-30% in older series.
  • Other poor prognostic factors: advanced age, cirrhosis, immunosuppression, delayed drainage and rupture.
  • Sepsis (organ failure) requires aggressive management with resuscitation, antibiotics and drainage. urgent.
  • Mortality in single uncomplicated abscesses is <5% if it is drained early.
  • Clinical improvement is evaluated with defervescence and decrease in leukocytes; Control tomography is not routine unless there is a bad outcome.
